hints: Focus on the word coherent in the stem - it has a precise definition involving frequency and phase difference.
Recall that phase difference can be constant at $0$, $\pi$ or any other fixed value, so ask whether in phase is the only possibility.
Check whether being transverse or having equal amplitude is part of that definition, or whether longitudinal sound and unequal amplitudes can still be coherent.
walkthrough: Identify the key term: the question asks what must be true for waves from two coherent sources.
State the definition of coherent: the sources emit waves of the same frequency and wavelength with a phase difference that is constant in time.
Note that constant does not mean zero: the fixed phase difference could be $0$, $180^{\circ}$ or any other value, so they are not necessarily in phase.
Note that the definition says nothing about wave type or size: coherent waves can be longitudinal like sound or transverse like light, and can have different amplitudes.
Therefore the only statement that must be correct is that they have a constant phase difference. This is option C.

options.A: In phase means zero phase difference, which is only one special case of coherence.
options.B: Coherent sound waves from loudspeakers are longitudinal, so coherence does not require transverse waves.
options.C: Coherent means same frequency and a phase difference $\phi$ that does not change with time.
options.D: Interference can still occur if amplitudes differ, though the minima will not be fully zero.
